Question: What is the least number of consecutive positive integers, that add up to 1000?
Answer: Let the first and last be F and L .  Then ( L − F + 1 ) ( L + F ) = 2000 = 2 4 ⋅ 5 3  The two terms in that product have opposite odd/even parity. One must be odd. We want L − F + 1 , the number of consecutive integers, to be as small as possible. If we made it even, we would have to include all the 2 s in its prime factorization. That would make it 16.  However, if we make it odd, we can use just one 5.  That’s as small as it can be. (Then the average (or middle value of the 5 ), ( L + F ) / 2 , must be 200. )

Question: What's the Monty Hall problem proof?
Answer: A2A: It’s not that hard to understand. Suppose your strategy is to switch. 1/3 of the time your initial guess will have been correct. So, when you switch, you lose. So 1/3 of the time you lose. For the 2/3 of the times when your initial guess was wrong, you win by switching. The odds are 2:1 in your favor. Suppose your strategy is to not switch. Then you win if and only if your initial guess was correct. That’s a 1/3 probability. The odds are 2:1 against you.

Question: A circle is cut on 2 pieces n times. With what probability will there be some specific m pieces?
Answer: A2A: We are making straight cuts across a disk. We assume that the cuts are chosen at random. So we can also assume that no more than two cut lines intersect at any point. It can be shown that the number of pieces added by a new cut is 1 plus the number of cut lines that the new cut crosses. So the total number of pieces will be 1 plus the number of lines plus the number of line intersections. We need to find the probability of line intersections. I will suppose that a random cut line is determined by randomly choosing two points on the circumscribing circle. The probability that two such randomly generated cuts intersect is 1 / 3. To see that, we’re choosing 4 points. The first 3 determine one line and an endpoint of the second line. They also determine 3 arcs separating those first 3 points around the circle. On average, the 4 th point (other end of second line) is as likely to fall on one of those arcs as another. However, there is only one of the arcs for which the second line will cross the first. We can assume that these 1 / 3 probabilities are independent for all line pairs. The expected number of pieces will be 1 + n + n ( n − 1 ) / 6. To get m pieces, we need m − 1 − n crossings. That probability is ( n ( n − 1 ) / 2 m − 1 − n ) ( 1 / 3 ) m − 1 − n ( 2 / 3 ) n ( n − 1 ) / 2 − m + 1 + n .

Answer: A2A: 101042 The concept applies to an ordering of any set of n distinct numbers. So let a n be the number of alternating orderings starting (or ending) on an up (or a down). (I.e., half the answer sought.) Letting a 0 = a 1 = 1 , then for, n > 1 , we can write a recurrence relation for a n based on the index k of the position for the minimum value of the set. There are ( n − 1 k − 1 ) ways to split all the other members of the set into two sets for those preceding position k and those following position k . For any such split, there are a k − 1 sequences ending on an up of the k − 1 to precede the minimum at k and a n − k starting on a down to follow. So 2 a n = ∑ n k = 1 ( n − 1 k − 1 ) ( a k − 1 a n − k ) Iterating that, I get the following sequence for 2 a n : 1 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 10 , 32 , 122 , 544 , 2770 , 15872 , 101042 To verify the above, I also wrote a Python script to count them by depth-first search for N > 1. Question: If unique random integers from 1-64 are placed on random squares of an 8x8 chessboard, what is the probability than and entire row or column has all prime numbers? Or that there exists a row/column such that the sum of all the numbers are prime?
Answer: A2A: Abstracting this: Let B ⊂ A be sets of size 18 and 64 and let R be a randomly chosen size 8 subset of A . Then the probability that R ⊂ B is ( 18 8 ) / ( 64 8 ) ≈ 0.00000989. B corresponds to a row or column. The probability that (without replacement) a second subset is also one of those other size 8 subsets is vastly smaller. So there is no significant error if we the regard full hits on those sets as being independent. So the probability that one of those rows or columns is hit is 16 ( 18 8 ) / ( 64 8 ) ≈ 0.00015818. (Any error from the independence assumption is much smaller than the rounding error on the last digit above.) In this answer, Lawrence Reeves reports that he ran a simulation that found a much larger apparent probability. So I thought I should take my own shot at a simulation. My Python script: Running that a few times convinced me that the answer would have to be close to 0.00016. For the second question, the expected value for the sum will be 260. So the probability of hitting a prime will depend on the density of primes in the vicinity of 260. Rather that approach that analytically, I also estimated that with a simulation: It reports probability p ≈ 0.1727 that a sum is prime. That’s 1 − p that one is not a prime, ( 1 − p ) 16 that none is prime, and a 1 − ( 1 − p ) 16 ≈ 0.9519 that at least one sum is prime.

Question: What is the difference between domain, support, codomain, range of a function?
Answer: A2A: The domain and codomain of a function are properties of the function that are specified in its definition. The function is defined for values in the set called its domain and its values must lie in a set called its codomain. The image of the function is the set of values in the codomain that are actually reached when the function is applied to all values in the domain. The image may be a proper subset of the codomain. Unfortunately, some use “range” to refer to the image and others use it to refer to the codomain. (Unless specified otherwise, I take ”range” to refer to the image.) When the image is a proper subset of the codomain, you can avoid the ambiguity by avoiding the use of “range” and using either “codomain” or “image” instead. (What typically matters is the image.) The support of a function is the subset of its domain for which the value of the function is non-zero.
